lines.text: Welcome. Today we look at fault ride-through: what a wind turbine must do when the grid voltage dips.
When a fault happens somewhere on the network, the voltage at the connection point can fall to a small fraction of normal for a few hundred milliseconds.
Older turbines simply disconnected. With a lot of wind on the system, that would turn a small fault into a large loss of generation.
So grid codes ask the plant to stay connected. That is low-voltage ride-through, LVRT.
Here is the curve. Time on the horizontal axis, voltage in per unit on the vertical axis.
Above the line the plant must stay connected. Below it, it may trip.
In this example curve, the voltage can fall to 0.15 per unit for 300 milliseconds, then must recover along this slope.
Staying connected is not enough. During the dip the plant should also inject reactive current to support the voltage.
The reactive current is usually a gain, K, times the voltage deviation, um, up to the converter's current limit.
After the fault clears, active power must come back within a set time. Too fast can shake the grid; too slow loses energy.
High-voltage ride-through is the mirror image: overvoltages after a fault, often up to about 1.2 or 1.3 per unit for a short time (?).
Now, how do we test this? Two ways: a field test with a voltage-dip container, and simulation with a validated model.
The container uses an impedance divider to create the dip at the turbine terminals without disturbing the whole grid.
Simulation results are only accepted when the model has been validated against those measurements.
A typical report shows voltage, active power and reactive current for each test case, on one page per case.
Common mistakes: plotting the wrong per-unit base, and checking only the depth of the dip but not its duration.
To sum up: stay connected above the curve, support the voltage during the dip, and recover active power at the right rate.

tldr: Grid codes require wind plants to stay connected through voltage dips and support the voltage.
Stay connected above the LVRT curve, inject reactive current during the dip, and restore active power at a set rate.
Compliance is shown by field tests with a voltage-dip container plus a validated simulation model.

points.text: Faults pull the voltage down for a few hundred milliseconds.
Mass disconnection of wind plants turns a small fault into a large generation loss.
Above the curve the plant must stay connected; below it, it may trip.
Example: 0.15 pu for 300 ms, then a recovery slope.
Reactive current = K x voltage deviation, up to the current limit.
Active power must recover within a set time after fault clearance.
A voltage-dip container uses an impedance divider at the turbine terminals.
Simulation counts only with a model validated against measurements.

visuals.title: Example LVRT curve
visuals.content:
| Time after fault (ms) | Minimum voltage (pu) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.15 |
| 300 | 0.15 |
| 3000 | 0.85 |

The plant must stay connected while the voltage is above the line.
visuals.meaning: Where the plant must stay connected

visuals.title: Reactive current during a dip
visuals.content: Delta I_q: extra reactive current (pu); K: gain (typically 2); Delta U: voltage deviation from nominal (pu); I_max: converter limit.
visuals.meaning: How much reactive current to inject

visuals.title: Voltage-dip container
visuals.content:
- Grid -> series impedance Z1 -> turbine terminals
- Switch S closes -> shunt impedance Z2 to earth
- Dip depth set by the ratio Z2 / (Z1 + Z2)
visuals.meaning: How a field test creates the dip

glossary.meaning: Low-voltage ride-through: staying connected through a voltage dip
High-voltage ride-through: staying connected through an overvoltage
Per unit: a value as a fraction of its base value

references.text: IEC 61400-21-1 (power quality and grid compliance measurement)
CEA technical standards for connectivity to the grid

procedure.step: Agree the test plan and cases with the utility
Run dip tests at low and high power
Validate the model against the measurements
Simulate the remaining cases with the validated model

claims.claim: HVRT limits are often around 1.2 to 1.3 pu
claims.why: Values differ between grid codes; check the one that applies

flashcards.front: What does LVRT require of a wind plant?
flashcards.back: Stay connected while the voltage stays above the grid code's LVRT curve.

flashcards.front: Why do grid codes require fault ride-through?
flashcards.back: Mass disconnection during faults would turn a small fault into a large loss of generation.

flashcards.front: How is reactive current during a dip usually set?
flashcards.back: A gain K times the voltage deviation, up to the converter current limit.

flashcards.front: What does a voltage-dip container use to create the dip?
flashcards.back: An impedance divider: series impedance plus a switched shunt impedance at the turbine terminals.

flashcards.front: When is a simulation accepted as compliance evidence?
flashcards.back: Only when the model has been validated against field measurements.

flashcards.front: Name two common plotting mistakes in FRT reports.
flashcards.back: Using the wrong per-unit base, and checking only the depth of the dip but not its duration.

added_context.text: 1 pu is the nominal value; 0.15 pu means 15 percent of nominal voltage.
